extracted.intended_audience: employers, immigration attorneys, state workforce agencies, labor economists, and other stakeholders affected by H-1B/PERM/EB visa prevailing wage determinations and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Federal Department of Labor proposed rulemaking on how to compute and publish prevailing wage levels for H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, PERM, and EB preference categories, including methodology, data sources, implementation scope, and economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent treatment across EB-3, EB-2, and H-1B
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the same wage methodology in multiple immigrant and nonimmigrant programs is important to ensure consistent treatment of similarly situated workers and prevent the creation of incentives for employers to prefer one classification over the other, because workers often have “one foot in each program” and the programs overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat EB-3 differently from EB-2 and H-1B because many H-1B workers adjust status through EB-3 and classifications are not mutually exclusive. Different wage methodologies across programs could cause sudden wage changes on status adjustment and encourage program shopping to the detriment of U.S. workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus adjustments on occupations with largest concentrations of alien workers
rubrics_metrics.description: In ascertaining wages paid to U.S. workers similarly employed to H-1B workers, the Department's analysis focused, to the greatest extent possible, on those occupations that account for 1 percent or more of the total H-1B population and which also account for a significant share of the PERM population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust wage levels with particular attention to occupations and visa classifications with the largest numbers of alien workers, because the risk of undercutting U.S. wages is greatest where concentrations of alien workers are larger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-tier wage structure with specified percentile targets
rubrics_metrics.description: The revised wage levels are set at approximately the 34th, 52nd, 70th, and 88th percentiles of the OEWS wage distribution for the most specific occupation and geographic area available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These percentiles replace the prior approximate percentiles (17th, 34th, 50th, 67th) to better align prevailing wages with experience, education, and supervision and to reduce adverse wage effects on U.S. workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation method for Levels I–IV
rubrics_metrics.description: Level I Wage is proposed to be calculated as the 34th percentile of the wage distribution; Level IV as the 88th percentile. Level II is determined by dividing the difference between Levels I and IV by three and adding the quotient to Level I. Level III is determined by dividing the difference by three and subtracting the quotient from Level IV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields Level II and Level III at approximately the 52nd and 70th percentiles respectively. The Department relies on the mathematical formula Congress provided for the intermediate levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) as primary prevailing wage source
rubrics_metrics.description: The BLS shall provide the OFLC Administrator with the OEWS wage data by occupational classification and geographic area, and the prevailing wage shall be based on the wage component of the OEWS survey in accordance with 20 CFR 656.40(b)(2)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OEWS data by occupation and geographic area is the default basis for PWDs and LCAs unless an employer provides an acceptable alternative survey or uses another permitted wage source (e.g., Davis-Bacon, SCA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual publication of prevailing wage rates on OFLC website
rubrics_metrics.description: The OFLC Administrator would publish, at least once in each calendar year, the prevailing wage rates produced under the new methodology as a notice posted on the OFLC website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing on the OFLC website is preferred because posting multiple prevailing wage rates in the Federal Register would be administratively burdensome; website posting is more user-friendly and allows employers and stakeholders to locate applicable wage data quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate reference to 'arithmetic mean' and specify BLS as OEWS administrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the regulation language to replace the term 'DOL' with 'BLS' when describing which entity administers the OEWS survey and remove references to the 'arithmetic mean' in describing how levels are calculated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By specifying the percentile-based computation directly in the regulation, the outdated reference to the arithmetic mean is removed and clarity is improved on the data source authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of private (employer) wage surveys in limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department proposes to retain private surveys as an option when government data sources do not fully capture niche labor markets or unique job requirements, but in limited circumstances and subject to methodological standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private surveys provide flexibility for specialized industries or geographic areas (benefit to start-ups/small businesses) but can be expensive and administratively complex; historically private surveys yield wages roughly 20% higher than OEWS-based wages. The Department will monitor and may reject surveys that do not meet methodological standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and prospective application of the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would apply to Applications for Prevailing Wage Determinations pending with the OFLC NPC as of the proposed effective date, and to PWDs submitted on or after the effective date and LCAs filed on or after the effective date where OEWS is the prevailing wage source and the employer did not obtain the PWD prior to the effective date. The Department does not propose applying the new regulations to previously-approved PWDs, permanent labor certification applications, or LCAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is applied prospectively to avoid retroactive changes to already approved determinations; employers with reliance interests are afforded latitude to adjust business practices accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPC responsibility for determining CBA coverage and prevailing wage when no CBA
rubrics_metrics.description: An NPC would continue to determine whether a job is covered by a collective bargaining agreement negotiated at arm's length. If not covered by such an agreement, an NPC would determine wages of workers similarly employed using the wage component of the BLS OEWS, unless the employer provides an acceptable survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This centralizes determinations at the NPC (non-agricultural PWDs are no longer processed by SWAs) and directs determinations to follow secs. 212(n), 212(p), and 212(t) of the INA consistent with revised 656.40(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevailing wages for lower-skilled occupations should approximate the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: For lower-skilled workers (jobs requiring limited skills or two years of training or less), meaningful differentiation based on skills is reduced; thus setting prevailing wages closer to the mean of the overall OEWS wage distribution is more appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because skill variation among lower-skilled occupations is limited, a mean-approximating wage better ensures similarly employed workers make similar wages. Examples: food service managers, meat processing workers, mushroom pickers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to EB-3 professionals (baccalaureate degree holders)
rubrics_metrics.description: EB-3 professionals, who typically hold bachelor’s degrees but less education/experience than EB-2 workers, are appropriately addressed by the adjusted wage levels; an entry-level wage at the 34th percentile is acceptable and may aid in certifying that no U.S. workers are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bachelor's degree credentials are relatively common in the U.S. workforce, placing an entry-level wage near the 34th percentile may slightly premium EB-3 wages but better supports the labor certification requirement to show insufficient willing, able, and qualified U.S. workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing reliance interests versus statutory mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department acknowledges employers' reliance interests in longstanding wage levels but determines that setting wage levels consistent with the INA and its purpose of protecting U.S. workers outweighs such interests; applying the methodology prospectively helps mitigate reliance burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adjusting long-standing regulatory practices, consider whether prior policy engendered serious reliance interests, but prioritize statutory alignment and the protection of U.S. workers if reliance interests conflict with statutory purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation of comments and preference for quantitative support
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department invites comments on all aspects of the proposed methodology, regulatory alternatives (including Experience Benchmarking), and other data sources; comments supported by reliable and objective data or quantifiable studies will be more helpful than qualitative anecdotal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders should submit evidence-based comments, especially data that can inform percentile selections, alternative surveys, or demonstrate reliance impacts; qualitative anecdotes are less persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department will monitor and may reject private surveys that fail methodological standards
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure integrity, the Department would monitor the use of private surveys to prevent abuse and reserves the right to reject any private survey that does not meet methodological standards or otherwise fails to satisfy regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers relying on private surveys must ensure survey methodology meets the Department's standards; anticipate scrutiny and potential rejection if methods are weak or results appear systematically high compared to OEWS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual notices will include OEWS survey area and SOC updates
rubrics_metrics.description: OFLC's routine annual announcement implementing updated OEWS prevailing wages will also discuss any other significant related updates, including changes to OEWS survey areas and relevant updates to the SOC system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should consult annual OFLC notices for survey area and SOC changes that could affect prevailing wage determinations, rather than relying on the Federal Register for multiple rate postings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory economic analysis conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory analysis covers a 10-year period (2026–2035), expresses impacts in 2024 dollars, and uses discount rates of 3% and 7% (pursuant to OMB Circular A-4); the Department estimates annualized costs and transfer payments and presents first-year and 10-year totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments on the economic analysis should address assumptions, data sources, methodologies, and potential differential effects by visa or program participation; the Department invites comment on unquantified benefits/costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost estimation inputs for rule familiarization
rubrics_metrics.description: For rule familiarization costs, the Department used the BLS mean hourly wage rate for private sector human resources specialists, adjusted to reflect total compensation by applying an overhead rate of 17% and a fringe benefits rate based on average total compensation to average wages and salaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating familiarization burdens, use job-relevant wage rates and include overhead and fringe adjustments consistent with the Department's method; the Department used FY data to calculate affected entity counts and hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory alignment requirement (8 U.S.C. 1182(p)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department determined the existing wage levels were not adequately aligned with the statutory requirement under 8 U.S.C. 1182(p)(4) to provide four wage levels commensurate with experience, education, and level of supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wage-setting must be consistent with statutory factors; methodologies that rely on outdated percentiles or data about workers not similarly employed may be in tension with the INA's intent to protect U.S. workers.
